title: U.S. goods trade deficit widens again as AI-led imports hit record high
html:
Shipping containers are docked at the port of Los Angeles in Long Beach, Calif., in March.Caroline Brehman/Reuters

The U.S. trade deficit in goods widened sharply in October as an AI infrastructure buildout boosted imports to a record high, potentially putting trade on course to again subtract from economic growth in the fourth quarter.

The surge in imports reported by the Commerce Department on Friday was also across other categories, including motor vehicles, industrial supplies and consumer goods, reflecting robust domestic demand. Imports have increased at a rapid clip despite President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariffs.

Trump has defended the duties as necessary to shrink the trade gap and rejuvenate the nation’s industrial base. The Trump administration this week proposed new maximum potential rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent on 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the European Union, to counter what the White House said was excess industrial capacity that these countries are promoting.

“The trade deficit in goods worsened in October, which will take a toll on economic growth in the fourth quarter,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “Capital goods imports are surging, showing that AI doesn’t always lead to greater U.S. economic growth.”

The goods trade shortfall jumped 10.7 per cent, or US$14.4-billion, to US$149.5-billion last month, the highest level since March 2025, the Commerce Department’s Census Bureau said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the goods deficit at US$133-billion.

Goods imports shot up 6.1 per cent, or US$21.1-billion, to US$365.3-billion, the highest level since the government started tracking the series in 1992. The broad increase in imports was led by capital goods, which soared 8.5 per cent. Capital goods increased 80.0 per cent on a year-on-year basis in October.

Businesses are aggressively spending on AI, giving the technology a prominent role in the economy. But the AI infrastructure buildout is heavily reliant on imports, which are a subtraction from gross domestic product growth.

Imports of consumer goods advanced 2.6 per cent while those of other goods increased 4.5 per cent. Domestic demand, which includes business investment and consumer spending, grew in the third quarter at its fastest pace in more than five years.

Imports of industrial supplies, which include crude oil and nonmonetary gold, increased 6.0 per cent last month, while those of motor vehicles, engines and parts accelerated 4.1 per cent. Imports of foods, feeds and beverages rose 2.5 per cent.

AI adding less to GDO growth

“This year’s surge in capital goods imports is one reason why AI is adding less to GDP than corporate spending figures suggest,” economists at Goldman Sachs wrote in a note.

Exports of goods increased 3.2 per cent, or US$6.7-billion, to US$215.8-billion. Exports of industrial supplies advanced 4.9 per cent and shipments of capital goods rose 3.4 per cent.

Exports of motor vehicles, engines and parts vaulted 5.7 per cent, while those of consumer goods increased 4.2 per cent. But exports of foods, feeds and beverages slumped 7.9 per cent.

The government reported on Wednesday that trade sliced off 3.21 percentage points from GDP growth in the third quarter. The drag was, however, more than offset by robust growth in consumer spending and business investment in equipment, mostly AI-related. The economy grew at a 4.3 per cent annualized rate last quarter after expanding at a 2.2 per cent pace in the April-June period.

Trade has not contributed to gross domestic product growth for four straight quarters, reflecting strong domestic demand.

The anticipated hit to GDP growth from trade this quarter could be blunted by businesses rebuilding inventories to meet demand.

The Census Bureau also reported on Friday that wholesale inventories increased 0.9 per cent in October after rising 0.8 per cent in September. Stocks at wholesalers were lifted by a 1.6 per cent jump in durable goods inventories. Retail inventories increased 0.8 per cent after climbing 0.7 per cent in September. Stocks at motor vehicle and parts dealers jumped 1.3 per cent after rising 0.6 per cent in September.

Excluding motor vehicles and parts, retail inventories increased 0.6 per cent last month after gaining 0.7 per cent in September. This component goes into the calculation of GDP.

Inventory investment rebounded in the third quarter after declining for five straight quarters. It added 1.64 percentage points to GDP growth last quarter.

Economists at Goldman Sachs lowered their fourth-quarter GDP growth estimate by 0.2 percentage point to a 2.2-per-cent rate. This estimate also factored in October’s wholesale and inventory data, which they said partly offset the drag from the large trade deficit.
summary: October deficit of more than 10% puts trade on track to weaken fourth-quarter GDP growth
